list.listitem: Use validated screening tools and the Resident Assessment Protocol to diagnose urinary incontinence (UI) in outpatient and nursing home settings, respectively. B
A careful history, a targeted physical examination, use of bladder diaries, urinalysis, and postvoid residual urine testing are recommended for the initial assessment of the patient with UI. B
A combination of lifestyle modification, behavioral therapy, and selective pharmacologic therapies is effective in the treatment of UI. B
Anticholinergic agents can be used for patients with urge UI and mixed UI. The choice of agent should be individualized and based on cost, side effects experience, and patient preference. A

background.definition: Urinary incontinence (UI) is an unintentional leakage of urine. Types of UI include stress incontinence (momentary leaking during coughing, sneezing, or laughing), urge incontinenelectroce (the loss of urine with a strong desire or urgency to void), and overflow incontinence (bladder is full and cannot empty due to obstructive or neurologic cause and overflows). Mixed incontinence is a combination of stress and urge incontinence and is most common in older women.

list.listitem: Thirteen million people in the United States have UI; 85% are women.
Fifty percent of nursing home populations 65 years and older, 50% of homebound elderly persons 65 years and older, and 25% to 30% of hospitalized elderly persons 65 and older have UI.

Twenty-five percent to 35% of community-dwelling persons 60 years and older have UI, as do 10% to 30% of younger adult women (between the ages of 15 and 64 years) and 1% to 5% of younger adult males (between the ages of 15 and 64 years).

A 2025 population-based study of U.S. women found that perceptions of suboptimal bladder health are widespread, with a median bladder health score of only 55 (on a 0–100 scale). Notably, 69% of participants reported using adaptive behaviors to manage their bladder function—such as "toilet mapping" (58%) or wearing pads (40%)—including 38% of women who were otherwise classified as asymptomatic.

A total of $16.4 billion is spent every year on incontinence-related care in the United States, including $11.2 billion spent on community-based incontinence programs at home, $5.2 billion on incontinence care in long-term facilities, and $1.1 billion on disposable products for adults.
Weakening or damage of urogenital muscles responsible for holding and/or releasing urine (eg, from birth trauma, pregnancy, menopause).
Neurologic disorders of the urogenital tract (eg, spinal cord injuries, multiple sclerosis, stroke, birth defects, aging).
Increased intra-abdominal pressure due to obesity.
Involuntary action of bladder muscles.
Psychophysiologic changes (eg, cognitive disorders, arthritis and coordination difficulties, mobility restrictions).
Transient causes, such as UTIs, cough with colds, and medications such as diuretics.
Obstructive causes, including fecal impaction, tumors, and urethral stones.

A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis found that hysterectomy is associated with significant long-term pelvic floor risks. Specifically, it is associated with an increased risk of pelvic organ prolapse after 10 or more years (adjusted Hazard Ratio 1.56).
In men, surgery such as transurethral, suprapubic laparoscopic, or radical prostatectomy.
Incontinence occurs when bladder pressure exceeds intraurethral pressure.
Factors that reduce intraurethral pressure include weak pelvic floor muscles and relaxed urethral muscle tone (the latter from decreased estrogen in the premenstrual or menopausal periods).
Increased bladder pressure may occur from involuntary bladder spasms due to detrusor muscle instability or neurologic defects.
Restricted mobility can make it difficult for patients to maintain continence.
In primary care settings, clinical history and symptom diaries are the most cost-effective methods of screening for UI in women. B
Screening programs should target patients at high risk of UI. B

The United States Preventive Services Task Force recommends a history and physical examination for screening, and simple office tests, including UA and postvoid residual testing, in the evaluation of UI. On average, 2 to 4 patients would be screened to detect 1 case of UI.
The Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality does not advise urodynamic studies such as cystoscopy, cystometrography, or imaging studies to screen for urinary incontinence.
Population-based surveys using validated scales yield a number needed to screen of 2 to 4 to detect 1 case of UI.

The Women's Preventive Services Initiative (WPSI) recommends annual screening of women for urinary incontinence annually, including an assessment of the presence of urinary incontinence and it affects on activities and quality of life.
Screening, assessment, and management of UI are mandatory for nursing home patients. Use the Minimum Data Set and Resident Assessment Protocol.

Validated surveys (in outpatient clinical settings) and the Resident Assessment Protocol included in the Minimum Data Set (in nursing home settings) are recommended to improve the accuracy of diagnosis of UI. B
Undertake cause-specific clinical evaluation of UI. C
UA is recommended in the initial UI evaluation to rule out other etiologies, such as infection, diabetes, or kidney stones. C
Postvoid residual volume is helpful to assess bladder contractility and the presence of bladder mechanical obstruction. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Dysuria, hematuria, frequency; symptoms resolve with treatment
Urgency, frequency, dysuria, nocturia, involuntary detrusor muscle hyperactivity and instability
Acute onset of irritative voiding symptoms within 1 to 2 months; microscopic hematuria
A positive phenazopyridine test turns urine (urinary incontinence) orange; there is no change in color if fluid is vaginal discharge

list.listitem: History should include an exploration of transient causes such as medication side effects (), acute worsening of medical conditions (eg, congestive heart failure) and UTI.

Once all transient causes have been ruled out, history should be used to determine UI category (ie, stress, urge, overflow, or mixed incontinence). See "Clinical decision rules" for a validated 3-item questionnaire.

Physical examination should include evaluation of: the pulmonary and cardiovascular systems to assess for fluid retention; the abdomen to assess for diastasis recti, masses, ascites, and organomegaly; the urogenital system to evaluate pelvic organs (for uterine prolapse), pelvic floor muscle tone (for weakness), vulva, and perineum (for inflammation, atrophy, urethral diverticula); the GI system to evaluate the anus and rectum (for bowel and pelvic growths, obstruction); and the neurologic system (eg, lumbosacral nerve root, bulbocavernosus, and clitoral sacral reflexes) to assess for sensory neurological lesions causing incontinence.

Stress incontinence in women can also be assessed by asking the patient to lie supine on the examination table with a full bladder, applying gauze to the perineum, and determining the presence of leakage following coughing, sneezing, or laughing. Lifting the urethra on both sides with the clinician's fingers should prevent urinary leakage.
Pad count (for urinary incontinence) is a poor measure or severity of urinary incontinence among both incontinent men and women.
Obtain a UA to detect hematuria (infection, malignancy, kidney stone), glucosuria (diabetes), pyuria, and bacteruria (UTI).

Postvoid residual testing can detect urinary retention (overflow incontinence) and can be measured by bladder ultrasound or urethral catheterization. A postvoid residual volume of more than 200 mL is considered abnormal, 50 to 200 mL is considered equivocal, and less than 50 mL is normal. Postvoid residual volume is highly variable and can be influenced by factors such as the volume voided before measurement, the time of day, whether the patient is ready to void or strains, and the efforts made by the patient to void the bladder completely. While it may influence clinical decision-making, the impact on clinical outcomes is not known.

Simple cystometry in the office using water instillation via a syringe into the urethra and bladder can be used to measure volume-related contractions; severe bladder contractions at less than 300 mL of bladder volume constitute urge incontinence. Simple cystometry is 75% to 100% sensitive, 69% to 89% specific, and has a 74% to 91% positive predictive value.

Refer for cystoscopy within 2 months of presentation for persistent irritative voiding symptoms (indicative of bladder neoplasm) or conditions resulting in persistent abnormal postvoid residual volume.

Other laboratory testing should be performed in the case of abnormal or inconclusive findings or treatment failure. Specialized urodynamic tests are available for patients requiring further evaluation (). When women with incontinence are assessed by urodynamics in addition to clinical methods, they are more likely to receive drug or surgical treatments. However, there is no evidence to show that they are less likely to be incontinent after treatment than women who did not have urodynamic testing.
A clinical decision rule has been developed and validated for the diagnosis of UI.

The key question is: During the last 3 months, did you leak urine most often: (a) when you were performing some physical activity, such as coughing, sneezing, lifting, or exercise? (diagnosis: stress); (b) when you had the feeling that you needed to empty your bladder, but could not get to the toilet fast enough? (diagnosis: urge); (c) without physical activity and without a sense of urgency? (diagnosis: other cause); or (d) about equally as often with physical activity as with a sense of urgency? (diagnosis: mixed).

Assess voiding and urine leakage history using a bladder diary; bladder diaries should include information about voiding episodes and urine volume, history of straining, discomfort, fluid intake, drugs (), recent surgery, and illness.
Use the history to determine the likely type of UI, and use the physical examination to identify possible causes.
Initial tests are UA and postvoid residual; subsequent testing is based on the type of UI and/or response to treatment and can include cystometry and cystoscopy (see and ).
Anticholinergic agents can be used for patients with urge UI and mixed UI. The choice of agent should be individualized and based on cost, side effects experience, and patient preference. A
Alpha-adrenergic agents can be used to treat stress incontinence. B
A combination of behavioral therapy (eg, pelvic floor exercise, scheduled toileting) and pharmacologic therapy is often the most effective way to treat UI. A
Abdominal retropubic urethropexies, sling procedures, and bulking-agent injections can be used to improve continence for women who fail drug therapy. B
Only about 1 in 8 to 1 in 12 patients with urge incontinence will achieve continence with typical treatments (fesoterodine, oxybutynin, and tolterodine). A

Patients with urge UI or mixed UI can be treated with an anticholinergic agent. A Cochrane systematic review showed that anticholinergic agents are more effective than placebo in the treatment of UI; treatment efficacy appears to be similar among agents within this class. Overall response to treatment, however, is limited (eg, decreased leakage by 1 episode every 2 days).

Options include nonselective anticholinergic agents (eg, oral short-acting oxybutynin 2.5-5.0 mg 3-4 times daily, long-acting oxybutynin 5-20 mg once daily, or transdermal patch) or a selective anticholinergic agent (eg, tolterodine 1-2 mg twice daily or 2-4 mg once daily). Short-acting oxybutynin is more effective than short-acting tolterodine, but the latter can be better tolerated.Transdermal formulations, which may cause cutaneous reactions, are not more effective in controlling UI than oral formulations. Long-acting formulations are more effective at controlling incontinence and have fewer anticholinergic side effects (ie, constipation, dry mouth, blurred vision, cognitive dysfunction) than their short-acting counterparts.The choice of agent should be individualized and based on cost, side effects experience, and patient preference.

Alpha-adrenergic agents (eg, phenylpropanolamine 25-100 mg twice daily in sustained-release form) are approved by the FDA for stress incontinence. Pseudoephedrine, with a similar mechanism of action as propanolamine, is sometimes used off-label to improve stress UI symptoms; however, there are no published studies demonstrating its efficacy in stress incontinence. A Cochrane review of 22 RCTs found weak evidence of improvement over placebo with reduced incontinence episodes and symptom improvement.

Among patients with overactive bladder (average of 8 or more micturitions per 24 hours and 3 or more significant urgency episodes with or without incontinence during a 3-day period), mirabegron (a beta3 receptor agonist given as a single dose of 50 or 100 mg once daily) was associated with one fewer incontinence episode every 2 to 3 days, improved quality of life scores, but no change in nocturia.
Nine RCTs demonstrated a 50% reduction in incontinence episode frequency and improved quality of life with the serotonin-noradrenaline receptor inhibitor duloxetine; long-term efficacy is unknown.

Among patients with enuresis, the tricyclic antidepressant (TCA) imipramine is as effective in reducing bedwetting as desmopressin (~1 fewer episode per night). However, TCAs have more side effects than desmopressin. Bedwetting alarms are more effective than TCAs, but require more effort on the part of the family and child to be effective.

In a meta-analysis of 4 randomized placebo-controlled trials of duloxetine vs. placebo for stress urinary incontinence (1913 patients), duloxetine was associated with 13% fewer weekly incontinence episodes, however the number of withdrawals for adverse effects of duloxitine were high (NNH = 7).
Other medications

Estrogens are shown to increase urethral vascularity and thickness and to improve alpha-adrenergic receptor sensitivity; both oral estrogen and estradiol-impregnated vaginal rings have been helpful in reducing overactive bladder symptoms related to inadequate estrogen levels. However, in both the Heart and Estrogen/Progestin Replacement Study and the Women's Health Initiative, postmenopausal women randomized to receive either estrogen alone or estrogen plus progestin had an increased risk of UI with an NNT to harm of 8 (ie, worsening of UI in 1 of 8 women treated).

In a phase 3 trial, vibegron, a β3-adrenergic receptor agonist, significantly improved overactive bladder (OAB) symptoms—including daily micturitions, urgency episodes, nocturia, and urge incontinence—in men with benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) undergoing treatment. Vibegron met all primary and secondary efficacy endpoints and was well tolerated, with similar adverse event rates to placebo.

Fesoterodine (Toviaz 4-8 mg daily) was associated with fewer nocturnal urgency symptoms and fewer nocturnal micturitions among 963 adults with urgency and frequency from overactive bladder. The absolute benefit was one fewer episode every 5 to 6 nights.

A recent meta-analysis concluded that typical treatments for urge incontinence (fesoterodine, oxybutynin, and tolterodine) restored continence in 8.5 to 13 women per 100 treated, and about 3% of patients with discontinue treatment due to adverse effects.

In an open-label randomized trial involveing 381 women, cystoscopic intradetrusor injection of 200 U of onabotulinumtoxinA (n = 192) was associated with a small improvement in daily eposides of incontinence compared to sacral neuromodulation (n = 189), and was associated witha higher risk of urinary tract infections and requirement for transient bladder self-catheterization.

Retropubic urethropexies, sling procedures, and bulking-agent injections (eg, glutaraldehyde cross-linked bovine collagen or carbon-coated beads) under the urethral bladder neck in the uroepithelium are used to support and move the bladder to improve continence.

Retropubic urethropexies (eg, Burch and Marshall-Marchetti-Krantz) and slings have long-term success rates of 85% to 96% for the treatment of stress incontinence. A Cochrane review of 13 trials, however, found insufficient evidence to determine whether slings were better or worse than other surgical methods or conservative management. Data on periurethral injection therapy are more limited but suggest efficacy.

A trial randomized 596 women with stress urinary incontinence to either a standard mid-urethral sling or a newer single-incision mini-sling. At 15 months, success was comparable (79% with mini-sling vs 76% with mid-urethral sling). At 36 months, success rates were 72% for the mini-sling and 67% for the mid-urethral sling (adjusted risk difference 5.7%, 95% CI -1.3 to 12.8%). At 36 months, there was a trend toward more subsequent surgeries in the mini-sling group (8.7% vs 4.6%, p = 0.12) and dyspareunia was reported significantly more often (11.7% vs 4.8%, p = 0.01).

Tension-free vaginal tape (nonabsorbable polypropylene mesh) has demonstrated reduced postoperative morbidity with 5-year success rates of greater than 86%. Tension-free vaginal tape is at least as effective as colposuspension for the treatment of urodynamic stress incontinence and appears to be more cost-effective. The long-term effects after 2 years are unknown.
Open retropubic colposuspension appears to be a more effective treatment for stress incontinence than anterior colporrhaphy or needle suspensions, especially over the long term.
Transurethral injection of bulking agents produces variable results.

For women undergoing pelvic organ prolapse surgery the benefit of adding a procedure to correct stress urinary incontinence (SUI) will reduce the likelihood of SUI postoperatively. There is a significant risk of postoperative voiding difficulties if a midurethral sling procedure is used as the incontinence procedure. There was no overall increase in complications with the use of a Burch colposuspension as the incontinence procedure.

Pelvic floor muscle training is of marginal effectiveness for women with UI. In 1 study, 38% of all patients with stress incontinence who performed Kegel exercises regularly for 3 months during specially supervised rehabilitation experienced a cure. However in another study of 175 primiparous women, weekly classes (for 16 weeks) of intensive pelvic floor muscle training was not associated with improvement in the presence of,nor frequency of, incontinence.

A 12-week randomized trial found that a pelvic floor-specific yoga program was not significantly more effective than a general physical conditioning program in reducing urinary incontinence (UI) episodes among women aged 45 and older.
A randomized trial failed to demonstrate a benefit of pelvic floor muscle training (weekly classes for 16 weeks) in postpartum women with UI at 6 months.

Bladder training, toileting assistance, and bladder drills are first-line treatments for urge incontinence and have shown up to a 50% improvement in overactive bladder symptoms and 20% dryness rate. Efficacy of bladder training for other types of UI is less impressive but the technique still appears helpful.

Pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) may be of small benefit for pregnant women without urine leakage to prevent leakage for up to 6 months after childbirth. However PFMT for women with urine leakage, it is uncertain if PFME reduces leakage.

Pelvic floor muscle training and behavioral modifications are recommended by some guidelines as first-line approaches for post-prostate treatment incontinence. However, in men having prostate surgery there is little evidence supporting the use of pelvic floor muscle training (with or without biofeedback) for treatment of UI after surgery, or for the prevention of UI before prostate surgery. In a Cochrane review, mens' symptoms improved over time irrespective of management.
Urinary catheterization (intermittent, indwelling, or suprapubic, depending on the severity of the clinical symptoms) is recommended for overflow incontinence.

Patients with chronic incontinence can be treated with scheduled toileting and prompted voiding. Improved access to toilets, managing fluids and diet, and using disposable garments can also be helpful.

Biofeedback, vaginal weight training, vaginal cones, and pelvic floor electrical stimulation to improve muscle tone and leakage have been shown to be useful for stress incontinence. Biofeedback has also been shown to be useful for urge UI and mixed UI.In 1 study, however, electrical stimulation did not add additional benefit to biofeedback.

In general, behavioral therapies—including bladder training, biofeedback, mindfulness-based stress reduction, yoga, and weight loss—are generally more effective than pharmacologic treatment for urinary incontinence in women.

A Cochrane review including 8 trials with 787 women concluded that there is little evidence on which to judge the efficacy of mechanical devices compared with no treatment, nor enough evidence to recommend any specific type of device for UI.

In a study of 504 women with stress urinary incontinence (SUI), 252 patients randomized to electroacupuncture of the lumbosacral region had less urinary leakage and fewer mean number of incontinence episodes than participants randomized to sham electroacupuncture (n = 252).
The extracorporeal magnetic innervation chair is an FDA-approved device, which provides a low-intensity magnetic field to strengthen the pelvic floor muscles in stress UI and mixed UI.
Untreated disease has been shown to have a negative impact on psychosocial functioning. Patients should be encouraged to recognize UI as a manageable and not shameful issue. A
Urinary incontinence may be a potential predictor of postpartum depression.

In men aged 50 to 69 with clinically localized prostate cancer who were randomized to recieve active surveillance reported better outcomes related to erectile dysfunction, incontinence and bowel function compared to those randomized to radiotherapy or surgical therapy. About 50% of men sho had surgery used at least one pad daily for 6 months, declining to ~20% at 4 years compared to no more than 12% in the other groups.

Untreated disease leads to continued bladder symptoms, limitations on mobility, and worsening quality of life and psychosocial functioning, and increased likelihood of secondary morbidities (eg, UTIs, skin maceration, and pressure ulcer formation).

In the Nurses' Health Study women experienced a high prevalence of urinary incontinence (eg, 17% of women age 39 - 56 reported severe urinary incontinence and 45% reported moderate incontinece). Only ~11% reported remission of symptoms on 10-year follow up. Higher body mass index and less physical activity were associated with progression of symptoms.
Symptoms and incontinence episodes can be improved with a combination of behavioral modifications and pharmacologic interventions targeted to the etiology and type of incontinence.
Screening questions, periodic office review of all current and new medications, and 24-hour bladder diary reviews can be used to assess symptoms and response to treatment.
UI is not an inevitable process of aging, nor is it shameful. It is treatable and manageable.
Among men treated for prostate cancer, ~12% regret their decision based in part upon the presence of "urinary bother."

cell.label: Basic evaluation for UI: • History (eg, risk factor assessment and bladder record/diary/severity index/3-item questionnaire, minimum data set) • Physical examination • Measure postvoid residual volume • Urinalysis.
Recurrent symptoms and unidentified causes should be further evaluated.

Options: -Bladder ultrasound -Radiography -Urodynamic tests () Urge and stress UI • Simple cystometry • Office stress testing • Multichannel or subtracted cystometrogram. Overflow UI • Voiding multichannel or subtracted cystometrogram • Pressure flow study • Uroflowmetry • Leak-point pressures and urethral pressure profiles • Electromyography.
Evaluate and treat reversible or transient conditions.

Transient causes (DIAPPERS): Delirium or confusional states • Infections of the urinary tract • Atrophic vaginitis or urethritis • Pharmaceuticals • Diuretics • Sedatives, anxiolytics, and alcohol • Beta-adrenergic blockers • Angiotensin-converting-enzyme inhibitors • Antidepressive and antipsychotic drugs • Psychological conditions (eg, depression) • Endocrine disorder (eg, hypercalcemia, hyperglycemia) • Restricted mobility, urinary retention • Stool (fecal impaction).

feature.caption: Diagnostics: Urodynamics Specialized Testing.
feature.feature_body:
Urge and Stress Incontinence
● Simple cystometry detects abnormalities of detrusor compliance and contractibility, measures postvoid residual, and determines capacity.
● Leak-point pressures and urethral pressure profiles are used to diagnose intrinsic sphincter deficiency.
● Multichannel or subtracted cystometrogram can differentiate involuntary detrusor contraction from an increase in intra-abdominal pressure; questionable accuracy.
Overflow Incontinence
● Voiding multichannel or subtracted cystometrogram or pressure flow study measures detrusor contractility and detects outlet obstruction.
● Uroflowmetry measures the urine flow rate; it is not helpful in diagnosing the types of incontinence found in women.
● Electromyography measures the integrity and function of urethral sphincter innervation.
Adapted from Urinary Incontinence in Adults, Clinical Practice Guideline Update. Rockville, MD: Agency for Health Care Policy and Research. March 1996.
